name: Retinyl esters
lead: Retinyl esters are fatty-acid esters of retinol (vitamin A), the main form in which the body stores vitamin A, chiefly as retinyl palmitate in the liver [2][3]. In cosmetics, retinyl palmitate, acetate and propionate are used as milder, more stable alternatives to retinol and tretinoin [4].

In skin, esters are described as converting to retinol and then to retinoic acid, though Wikipedia states neither absorption nor conversion is very efficient [4]. No trials of retinyl esters for cosmetic appearance were found in the sources reviewed.

paras: Dietary retinoids are needed for growth, vision, immune function, reproduction and skin barrier function, and the body must obtain them from food [3]. Retinol is esterified by LRAT for storage and released by retinyl ester hydrolases; hormone-sensitive lipase can hydrolyze retinyl esters [2][4]. Retinyl esters also act as substrates in the visual cycle, where RPE65 converts them toward 11-cis-retinal [1][4].

No studies found of retinyl esters used on skin for appearance. Related work covers vitamin A status and absorption, for example a registered trial of vitamin A absorption from fortified bouillon [5].

Preformed vitamin A in excess can cause hypervitaminosis A [4]. Retinyl palmitate in sunscreens drew public debate after animal studies in which topical retinyl palmitate or retinoic acid increased tumor rates in UV-exposed mice. A 2010 toxicological analysis reported no convincing evidence that retinyl palmitate is carcinogenic in sunscreens, while a later National Toxicology Program report on SKH-1 mice found worsened tumor rates [4].

card.summary: Vitamin A's storage esters, used in creams as gentler retinol alternatives; skin evidence is thin.
card.note: Sunscreen-use safety debated; excess vitamin A is toxic.

quick.overview:
Retinyl esters are the form in which the body stores vitamin A, also used in cosmetics as milder retinoid ingredients.

No trials in the sources reviewed tested them for appearance.
quick.mechanism: In skin they are described as converting to retinol and then retinoic acid, though conversion is said to be inefficient.
quick.risks: Excess preformed vitamin A causes hypervitaminosis A. Sunscreen use of retinyl palmitate prompted a mouse-study debate.
